Our results support that the knots in the jets are indeed produced by semi-periodical variations in jet velocity, so that the shock-forming model can be used to determine the velocity and inclination angle of the jets from the SiO knots.

The data are part of the ALMA Survey of Orion Planck Galactic Cold Clumps (ALMASOP) project (cite: 2020ApJ...898..107H; 2020ApJS..251...20D; 2021ApJ...907L..15S), in which only these six targeted sources were seen with clear periodical knotty structures.

However, it requires multi-epoch observations with enough spatial and velocity resolution over several years to measure the jet proper motion in order to derive the jet velocity. In addition, inclination angle of the jet, which is also needed to derive the jet velocity, can not be measured directly. Here we employ a novel method to constrain both the inclination angle and the jet velocity, requiring only one epoch of observation.

Notice that, in order for this model to work, the jets must have at least a few roughly equally spaced knots produced by internal shocks. In addition, the shock speed ($\Delta V$) should be around 10 to 40 km s$^{-1}$ (cite: 1997A&A...321..293S), so that the SiO emission is indeed produced by shocks. Moreover, no significant energy is dissipated in the shocks so that the thermal energy produced by the shocks can be totally transferred sideways into the sideways ejection.

Some asymmetry is seen in the ambient material in the C$^{18}$O total intensity maps around the sources (Figure [2](#outflow) (a) to (d)), however, further observations at a larger scale are needed to check it.
